newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - U.S. states reach agreement with Prudential.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.S. states reach agreement with Prudential.

text.p: Florida, Texas and Massachusetts reached separate multi-million dollar agreements on Thursday with Prudential Insurance Co of America, settling allegations the firm used deceptive sales practices to sell life insurance.
Prudential agreed to pay Florida $15 million, Massachusetts $2.4 million and Texas $2 million and improve a restitution offer to consumers.

The agreements will make it easier for consumers nationwide to qualify for relief and will enable people who were 60 years or older at the time of the alleged deception to get the maximum amount of relief available.
For Prudential, the deals help bring the Newark, N.J.-based insurer another step closer to putting its sales practice problems behind it.
"We're happy to have reached agreements with these states and are happy we can begin the process of resolving the problems of our policyholders in these states," a Prudential spokesman said.
The three states along with California in December urged a federal judge to reject a class-action settlement by Prudential, calling it unfair to consumers.

Under that settlement, reached in September, Prudential agreed to pay at least $410 million to as many as 10.7 million policyholders who bought permanent life insurance policies between 1982 and 1995.
The proposed class-action settlement could cost Prudential as much as $1.2 billion in direct expenses and could have a total value to the policyholders of almost $2 billion.
A hearing to determine the fairness of the proposed settlement is scheduled to begin on Monday in the U.S. district court in Newark, N.J.
One of the lead attorneys for the plaintiffs in the class action said he welcomed the settlement.
"I think it's an endorsement of my settlement," said Melvyn Weiss of the New York law firm Milberg Weiss Bershad Hynes & Lerach.
"I always felt that any improvements that they could make that would help the class members would be welcomed by me," he said.
The class-action settlement followed an agreement Prudential reached last in the last northern summer with a multi-state task force of insurance regulators.
Insurance regulators for 43 states and Washington D.C. had recommended a $35 million fine and a restitution program.
The payments under the latest agreements were considered large -- with the $15 million to Florida nearly half the size of the multi-state fine -- but not a threat to Prudential's financial capacity.

The Florida payment includes a fine and costs, Prudential said. The Massachusetts payment includes $1.2 billion in fines and $1.2 billion to the state attorney general's office for monitoring the settlement process.

"They're a lot as fines go," A.M. Best vice president Michael Albanese said. "Relative to Prudential's financial capacity, it's very manageable. But they are very, very large fines from a regulatory standpoint," he said.
However, the agreements with the three states may help smooth the way for Prudential at Monday's fairness hearing.
At least one of the states, Texas, has said it will withdraw its objection to the proposed class-action settlement.
"Forward progress had been sort of seized up as a result of the holdout states," Standard & Poor's analyst David Havens said.
"The fact that Florida as well as some of the others have now come on board allows Prudential to move forward and try and expedite the ultimate resolution of this whole chapter," he said.
California is now left as the only state that has not struck a deal to settle with Prudential.

A California insurance department spokeswoman said the department was continuing its special investigation of Prudential's sales practices and was working aggressively to get the highest return for California consumers.
Florida had been one of the most outspoken critics of Prudential's proposed class-action settlement of consumer sales complaints.
But state officials said in Tallahassee that Florida would now drop its opposition.
